On the morning of his first board presentation in Lisbon, Ivan's hands were cold and his heart was banging. In the lift the old thought arrived: I feel this bad, so it's going to go badly.

He stopped it, the way he'd practised. "I feel anxious," he said under his breath. "That's a feeling. The meeting hasn't happened yet." He named what he knew instead: the numbers were checked twice, Gabriel had heard him rehearse on Friday, the slides worked.

Gabriel was waiting outside the room. "Nervous?"
"Very," Ivan said. "And ready. Both."

He went in with the nerves still there, like a dog at his heels, but not holding the lead. His voice shook for the first minute, then steadied. When the chairwoman asked a hard question, he answered it. Afterwards Gabriel grinned. "You looked calm."
"I wasn't," Ivan said. "But I didn't let it drive."

qa.q: Who had heard Ivan rehearse on Friday?
qa.a: Gabriel had heard him rehearse on Friday.

qa.q: How did Ivan feel in the lift, and what did he tell himself?
qa.a: Ivan felt anxious, with cold hands and a banging heart, and told himself that feeling anxious is not the same as the meeting going badly.

qa.q: What did Ivan do to keep the feeling from steering?
qa.a: He named the feeling, listed the facts (checked numbers, rehearsal, working slides), and went ahead with the plan.

qa.q: How did Gabriel see Ivan afterwards?
qa.a: Gabriel saw him as calm and was pleased, not knowing how nervous Ivan still felt inside.

grounding: Shows a young man who tells himself that feeling anxious before a board meeting is not the meeting going badly, and proceeds.

The parent-teacher meeting at the Lucknow school started at ten, and by nine thirty Deepika's stomach was in knots. It was her first year as class teacher of 7B, and Mr Saxena, who had complained twice by email, was coming.

In the staff room she caught the thought: I'm this anxious, so it's going to be a disaster. She'd learned to answer it. She took out a card and wrote: Feeling: anxious. Fact: I have his son's marks and three examples of improvement. Plan: listen first, then show the examples.

Nirmala, the senior teacher, saw the card. "Good card. Want me nearby?"
"Just in the corridor," Deepika said.

In the meeting her voice shook at first. Mr Saxena was sharp, then quieter as she showed the improvement in his son's essays. At the end he said, "I didn't know he was trying." Deepika left still shaky, but with a plan agreed.

qa.a: The meeting started at ten.

qa.q: What did Deepika feel before the meeting, and how did she respond to it?
qa.a: Deepika felt anxious, her stomach in knots, and reminded herself that the feeling was not proof the meeting would go badly.

qa.q: What did Deepika's card do?
qa.a: It separated feeling (anxious) from fact (marks and examples) and a plan (listen, then show), so the anxiety didn't steer.

grounding: Shows a young teacher who separates her anxiety about a tough parent meeting from the facts and follows her plan.

Dear Sarita,

You asked how the meeting with the housing society committee went. It went fine. But I want to tell you about the hour before.

I was so anxious my hands were trembling. The old voice said, "You feel terrible, so you're going to mess this up." Remember what you told me last year? "Feelings are weather, not forecasts." So I sat on the stairs and said it plainly: I'm anxious. That's real. And the facts are: the leak is from their pipe, I have photos, and I've asked politely twice.

I let myself feel scared for a few minutes. I didn't argue with it. Then I went in anyway, photos in hand. My voice wobbled once. The secretary looked at the photos and said they'd fix it by next week.

Thank you for the weather line. I carry it everywhere now.

Jahnavi

Class teacher's note, Class 5A, 12 September.

Hrithik came second in the maths test today, one mark behind Neel. He did not cry, but he pressed his lips together so hard they went white, and he tore a corner off the paper. At break he told me, "I must always be first. And boys must never cry. I broke both rules today."

He says "I must" and "I should" often, and looks tense even when he does well.

I told him that second is a good result, and that anyone, boy or girl, is allowed to cry. I asked him to try changing "must" to "would like to" for one week. He looked doubtful.

I will speak gently to his parents on Friday about easing the pressure together.

Darshan

qa.a: Hrithik was one mark behind Neel.

qa.q: Why does coming second make Hrithik feel he broke the rules?
qa.a: Hrithik feels ashamed and tense, because his rigid rules say he must always be first and never cry.

qa.q: What small change did Darshan suggest, and why?
qa.a: Changing "must" to "would like to" for a week, which softens the rules so a slip doesn't pile up shame.

qa.q: How might Neel feel about coming first?
qa.a: Neel is probably pleased, with no idea that Hrithik felt a rule had been broken.

grounding: A teacher's note records a boy who tells himself he must always be first and never cry, and feels ashamed at any slip.

At the district sports day near Bathinda, Yamini came second in the 400 metres. Gurleen, who came fourth, hugged her. "Silver! Your first medal!"

Yamini didn't hug back. "I should have come first. I always should. Papa once said a Sidhu never comes second." Her eyes stung, and she scrubbed them hard. "And I shouldn't cry either."

Gurleen stared. "Who says you shouldn't cry?"
"Nobody. I just shouldn't."

They sat under the peepal tree while the relay started. Gurleen said, "If I had your rules, I'd feel bad every single day."
Yamini laughed wetly. "I do."

That evening Papa saw the silver medal and swung Yamini up in the air. "Silver! My girl!" Yamini blinked. Maybe the rule had been louder in her head than in his.

qa.a: Yamini came second.

qa.q: Why did Yamini scrub her eyes so hard?
qa.a: Yamini felt ashamed and upset about coming second, and her rigid rule said she shouldn't cry either.

qa.q: What could help Yamini ease her rules?

I'm Joseph, and last year I spent my whole birthday week angry at everyone. My mother, Bhavna, should have known I wanted a small party with friends, not the usual family dinner. I'd dropped hints, sort of. And my friends should have kept the day free. Two of them had tuition. One went to a wedding.

I didn't say anything. I just got colder each day. When Amma asked what I wanted, I said, "Nothing," and then felt furious that nothing is what I got.

On the night, after the family dinner, I finally exploded: "Nobody in this house understands me!" Amma looked shocked. "Joseph, you said nothing. How could I understand?"

That sentence stuck. I'd built rules in my head, parents should read my mind, friends should drop everything for me, and then punished everyone for breaking rules they'd never heard of.

This year I told Amma what I wanted. We had the party.

qa.q: What did Joseph answer when Amma asked about birthday wishes?
qa.a: Joseph said, "Nothing."

qa.q: Why did Joseph grow colder each day of the birthday week?
qa.a: Joseph felt resentful and unseen, holding unspoken rules that parents should read minds and friends should drop everything.

qa.q: What changed this year, and why did it work?
qa.a: Joseph told Amma directly what was wanted, which turned hidden expectations into a plan they could share.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt when Joseph exploded?
qa.a: Bhavna was shocked and probably hurt, having asked and been told "Nothing".

grounding: A teenager looks back on expecting a parent to read their mind and friends to always be free, and the resentment it built.
